clinicalPearls: Dressler syndrome is a delayed, immune-mediated pericarditis (a form of post-cardiac injury syndrome) that classically develops weeks to a few months after myocardial infarction, cardiac surgery or other myocardial or pericardial injury.

It should be distinguished from early peri-infarction (epistenocardiac) pericarditis, which occurs within the first few days of infarction and reflects direct transmural inflammation rather than an immune mechanism.
Its incidence has fallen markedly in the reperfusion era, as prompt revascularisation limits the extent of myocardial injury and antigen exposure.
The typical picture combines pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward, low-grade fever, a pericardial friction rub, a pericardial and/or pleural effusion and raised inflammatory markers.

Diagnosis rests on the clinical syndrome supported by ECG (diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression), echocardiographic effusion and elevated CRP/ESR, in the appropriate temporal context after cardiac injury.
First-line treatment is high-dose non-steroidal anti-inflammatory therapy (aspirin is often preferred after recent myocardial infarction) combined with colchicine, which reduces recurrence.

Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory or contraindicated cases because they are associated with a higher recurrence rate and, early after infarction, theoretical concern regarding myocardial healing.
Recognised complications include recurrent pericarditis, large effusion with tamponade and, rarely, constrictive pericarditis.
reference.pathophysiology: Dressler syndrome is understood as an autoimmune or immune-mediated inflammatory response triggered by injury to the myocardium and pericardium. Necrosis exposes previously sequestered cardiac (particularly pericardial and myocardial) antigens to the immune system, and in susceptible individuals this provokes the formation of anti-heart antibodies and a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. The resulting immune complex-mediated and cell-mediated inflammation involves the pericardium and frequently the adjacent pleura and lung, producing a pericarditis often accompanied by pericardial and pleural effusions and occasionally pulmonary infiltrates. The characteristic latent interval of weeks to months reflects the time required to mount this adaptive immune response, distinguishing it mechanistically from the immediate, direct inflammation of early peri-infarction pericarditis.
additionalDifferentials: recurrent or reinfarction / acute coronary syndrome
pneumonia or pleurisy of other cause
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG (diffuse concave ST elevation, PR-segment depression)
inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) and full blood count
chest radiography (cardiomegaly, pleural effusion, pulmonary infiltrate)
cardiac troponin to help exclude reinfarction
cardiac MRI in equivocal cases (pericardial inflammation/enhancement)
cross-sectional imaging or catheterisation if constriction is suspected
redFlags: hypotension with raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus indicating tamponade
large or rapidly accumulating pericardial effusion
features suggesting reinfarction or a new acute coronary syndrome rather than pericarditis
haemodynamic compromise in a patient on anticoagulation with a growing effusion
signs of evolving constrictive physiology (progressive right heart failure, raised venous pressure)
reference.prognosis: With appropriate anti-inflammatory therapy the syndrome is usually self-limiting and carries a good prognosis, though recurrences are not uncommon; serious sequelae such as tamponade or constrictive pericarditis are infrequent but clinically important.
pitfalls: Confusing delayed Dressler syndrome with early peri-infarction pericarditis, which differ in timing, mechanism and implications.
Overlooking tamponade in a patient on anticoagulation after myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery.
Reaching for corticosteroids first line, given their association with higher recurrence rates.
Attributing recurrent post-infarction chest pain solely to ischaemia and missing the pericardial nature of the pain.
Omitting colchicine, which reduces the risk of recurrence when added to anti-inflammatory therapy.
